label: Gromov-Witten Invariants
notes: Chapter 7 spans printed pages 201 through 256 and converts the moduli machinery of earlier chapters into deformation-stable numbers. We motivate genus-zero invariants as virtual counts of J-holomorphic spheres meeting fixed constraints, and preview how the axioms recover classical enumerations of rational curves in projective space.

label: From Curves to Counts
notes: A Gromov-Witten invariant is not a literal count of visible curves but an oriented intersection number. We pull back chosen cohomology classes under the evaluation maps and integrate over the virtual fundamental class of the compactified moduli space, so the answer depends only on the homology class and degrees.

label: The Evaluation Map
notes: Each marked point gives an evaluation map sending a stable map to the image of that point in the target. Pulling back constraint classes and pairing the product against the moduli cycle turns geometry into intersection theory, and this construction is the technical heart of the genus-zero definition.

label: The Dimension Gate
notes: Before a moduli problem can be a number, its constrained dimension must vanish. For degree d spheres in the projective plane the stable-map dimension is 3d plus k minus one, and each point constraint removes complex codimension two, isolating curves exactly when k equals 3d minus one.

label: Constraints as Cycles
notes: We visualize a sphere meeting submanifolds Poincare dual to the constraint classes alpha_i. The evaluation map records where each marked point lands, and requiring those images to lie on fixed generic cycles cuts the moduli space down to the finite oriented set whose signed cardinality is the invariant.

label: Pseudocycles and Semipositivity
notes: For semipositive manifolds the evaluation map defines a pseudocycle whose boundary strata have codimension at least two, so it carries a well-defined homology class. Indecomposable classes prevent the count from leaking into lower-energy bubbles, giving a rigorous count without the full virtual cycle technology.

label: Invariance
notes: The invariant is independent of the generic almost complex structure and of the chosen geometric representatives of the constraints. A generic path of structures supplies an oriented cobordism between the two finite solution sets, so the signed count is preserved and the number is a genuine symplectic invariant.

label: The Obstruction Bundle
notes: When a convenient almost complex structure is nonregular, excess dimension is absorbed by a finite-rank obstruction bundle whose fibers are cokernels of the linearized operator. A generic section vanishes on a set of expected dimension, and its Euler class replaces the direct count of regular curves.

label: The Gromov-Witten Axioms
notes: The axioms make the invariants a structured intersection theory. The effective axiom kills negative-area classes, the fundamental-class and divisor axioms simplify special insertions, and grading enforces the dimension test. Together they constrain the invariants tightly enough to make many of them computable by hand.

label: Splitting and Gluing
notes: The splitting axiom evaluates a nodal boundary by summing over decompositions of the class into two pieces glued along a Poincare-dual basis of the diagonal. A domain degeneration in the moduli of four marked spheres equates two boundary divisors and produces the fundamental gluing relation.

label: WDVV and Kontsevich Recursion
notes: Keel's description of boundary relations in the moduli of marked genus-zero curves yields the WDVV equation for the potential. Extracting the degree d coefficient for the projective plane gives Kontsevich's recursion, which assembles each count from products of lower-degree splittings along the diagonal.

label: Counting Rational Plane Curves
notes: The recursion reproduces the classical enumerations of rational curves in the projective plane: one line through two points, one conic through five, twelve cubics through eight, and six hundred twenty quartics through eleven. These exact integers are the chapter's concrete payoff and validation.
